entries.subject: peacock butterfly larva
entries.title: The bit with everybody
entries.body:
Pip had found the tender part of the nettle. He told all of us.

I got there late. By then there was a caterpillar across the edge, another under it, and one eating with the calm of someone who had never had to announce where his rear end was. I squeezed between two of them. The leaf tilted. Everyone held on, except Pip, who had to stop eating and hang there looking surprised.

I wanted to help. I took a bite to make myself smaller. This was not sound reasoning, but at the time I was a caterpillar.

Eventually Pip got back onto the leaf. There was almost nothing left of the tender part. I backed away from the last piece and let him have it.

He ate it without thanking me. Then pointed us toward another leaf.

I got there first this time. I saved him the edge.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly
entries.title: The first warm patch
entries.body:
The sun reached the dry stems and I opened my wings. All of them. Farther than I intended. There was suddenly an enormous amount of me exposed to the morning.

A stem shifted underneath my feet. I closed everything in a hurry. Nothing happened. The stem had been a stem the whole time.

I opened again, a little more slowly. Red spread out on either side. Warmth arrived where there had only been weight. I stayed there long enough to stop thinking about how I looked from above.

Then I tried to leave. Caught one foot on the stem. Pulled. Turned halfway around before it came free.

My first grand departure involved briefly facing the wrong direction. The second was wonderful. I went much too far and had to find another place to sit.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly
entries.title: The other guest
entries.body:
There was someone else on the white flower. Small, quick, already feeding.

I landed on the next head and waited. I thought this was considerate. The flower bent toward theirs. Now I was closer. I tried shifting my weight away, which brought one whole wing across the space between us.

They flew up. I froze. They came down on the other side and went straight back to feeding.

For a while we managed it. Each of us going around our own little patch, the stem gently bobbing beneath us. Then I reached the side they'd started on and found almost nothing left.

I was about to feel wronged when they reached my side.

We both left. In opposite directions. A perfectly civil meal, considering neither of us had intended to share.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly
entries.title: The stone stayed
entries.body:
I landed on the pale stone because it was warm. After the stems and flowers, its stillness felt enormous.

Nothing bent when I settled. Nothing tipped. I opened my wings and the stone continued being there, with no visible effort at all.

I stayed longer than I meant to. A shadow passed, and I closed my wings. Then opened them again. The stone didn't mind either way.

Eventually I lifted off. Circled once. Came back to the same patch, though there were other stones and perfectly good flowers nearby.

I don't know what it is like to be able to stay. I keep leaving things. Sometimes before I'm ready.

I sat until the warmth began to fade. Then I found a flower, drank far too much, and nearly came back to tell the stone about it.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly
entries.title: The quiet leaf
entries.body:
I went back toward the nettles. Not because I wanted to eat them. I couldn't have done it properly now if I'd tried. I wanted the place where there had always been somebody else chewing.

I landed on a fern instead. It held me. There was no familiar scraping, no black spiny back pushing past, no Pip with a new leaf to announce.

For a while I opened and closed my wings without leaving. I had more sky than I had ever wanted when I lived among the nettles. I would have exchanged a little of it for an interruption.

Then the fern tipped under me in the breeze. I gripped harder and almost laughed. There it was: the old feeling of having picked somewhere that could not quite be trusted with my weight.

I stayed for another gust.

entries.subject: pixie's parasol fungus
entries.title: The drop
entries.body:
The drop arrived gently. That was the misleading part.

It settled in the middle of my cap, round and bright. A little piece of the light moved around inside it. I held it there while other drops fell past. This one seemed to have chosen me.

Then a second drop joined it. The bright thing grew. My cap dipped. I waited for the water to notice that I was not very large.

Another drop. The edge tilted, and all of it slid off at once.

I sprang back so suddenly that the little fleck of bark beside the hollow jumped too. For a moment I was empty, upright and offended. Then I missed the moving light.

The next drop arrived. I let it stay. I am apparently the sort of fungus that has to learn something more than once, in the same patch of rain.

entries.subject: pixie's parasol fungus
entries.title: Three appearances
entries.body:
Three of my caps came through the wood. Not at once. One, then another, then the third after a long stretch when I thought it might not manage.

A fleck of bark rested on the middle one. The smallest leaned. The largest had a dark little hollow that held the light differently. I had done this before, but never exactly these three.

Someone knelt nearby. Their shadow covered us. For a moment I felt absurdly protective, though I was still mostly inside the wood and could not pull a cap back in.

They moved closer. Stopped. Moved away without touching anything.

I remained tense for a while. Then the light came back onto the smallest cap. It was still leaning.

I had imagined wanting an impressive appearance. It turned out I wanted three unimpressive ones left alone to finish.

entries.subject: wolf's-milk slime mold
entries.title: They disagreed
entries.body:
Two people stopped beside the log and disagreed about what I was.

One was quite certain. The other bent closer. Then the first bent closer too, apparently unwilling to lose by being further away.

I remained pink. The older bodies beside me remained gray. This seemed to complicate matters. A finger approached, paused and withdrew. I was grateful for that much caution, whatever name it belonged to.

They stayed for a while. Their shadows covered the log, and the dampness lasted longer than it had in the open light. By then I was beginning to enjoy the disagreement. They were very earnest about understanding me. I was mainly enjoying not drying out.

Eventually they stood up and left, still unconvinced.

The sun came back. I found myself wishing they would return with someone even less certain.
